question: Has India really ended poverty? What the World Bank's 2026 report shows, and why economists still argue

theme.label: Economy and public money
readerQuestions: What is the headline economic number?
Is this a total number or a per-person number?
How much of the story is prices, exchange rates, or GDP share?
What does this explain about household life?

plannedCharts.title: Almost no Indian is below the lowest poverty line now. Four in five are below the higher one
plannedCharts.subtitle: Share of Indians below each World Bank line, 1990-2030 · price-adjusted (PPP) dollars a person a day, 2021 prices · dots are survey years; after 2024 the lines are estimates
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The whole answer in one picture: the lowest line has almost emptied, the highest has not.

plannedCharts.title: The world's fall in extreme poverty stalled after 2019. India's kept going
plannedCharts.subtitle: Share of people below $3 a day (2021 PPP dollars), 1990-2026 · World Bank estimates; 2025-26 are estimates, and India's 2015-21 values are filled in without survey data
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Places India's fall against a world where progress has stopped.

plannedCharts.title: India has 18% of the world's people, 4% of its extremely poor, and 30% of everyone below $8.30
plannedCharts.subtitle: India's share of the world's poor at each World Bank line in 2024, beside its share of world population · 2021 PPP dollars
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Shows why India drops out of the extreme-poverty story and becomes the centre of the wider one.

plannedCharts.title: A 10% fall in spending would push the share of Indians below $4.20 a day from 15% to 23%
plannedCharts.subtitle: Share of Indians below each line in 2024, and after a hypothetical 10% fall in everyone's spending · 2021 PPP dollars
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Shows how many people sit just above each line.

plannedCharts.title: 47% of people in Jharkhand live below $4.20 a day. In Goa, under 3% do
plannedCharts.subtitle: Share of people below $4.20 a day (about Rs 95) by state and union territory · World Bank subnational atlas, 2023 reference year, from HCES 2023-24
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Shows where the poor are concentrated.

plannedCharts.title: In every state, small children are more likely than the average resident to live in a poor household
plannedCharts.subtitle: Share below $8.30 a day, children aged 0-5 against everyone, 14 selected states · World Bank state estimates from the 2023-24 household survey
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Poverty falls hardest on households with young children.

plannedCharts.title: India has less extreme poverty than Bangladesh or Indonesia, but more people below $8.30
plannedCharts.subtitle: Share of people below each line in 2024 · 2021 PPP dollars · Indonesia from a 2024 survey, the others are estimates
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Tests India's record against its neighbours at every line.

plannedCharts.title: Poor Indians work almost the same hours as everyone else
plannedCharts.subtitle: Average weekly hours of people in work, by household above or below $3 a day · India, 2024 · World Bank
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Rules out laziness or idleness as the explanation.

plannedCharts.title: Poor workers are more often self-employed and on farms
plannedCharts.subtitle: Share of workers, by household above or below $8.30 a day · India, 2024 · World Bank
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: What differs is the kind of work, not the amount.

plannedCharts.title: Since 2014-15, real GDP per person has grown 62%. A farm labourer's real wage has grown 9%
plannedCharts.subtitle: Real GDP per person and real daily wages, 2014-15 = 100 · rural wages for men (Labour Bureau, CPI-Rural), factory wage per day worked (Annual Survey of Industries, CPI-Combined) · rural 2019-20 and 2020-21 incomplete
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Tests whether growth reached the pay of the people most likely to be poor.

plannedCharts.title: If poor households had better-off households' jobs and pay, the share below $8.30 would fall from 79% to 57%
plannedCharts.unit: % of population or of the line
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank simulation for India, 2024 · share of people below each line and how far below it they are, now and simulated
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Sizes the jobs route out of poverty.

plannedCharts.title: New price data raised India's extreme poverty rate and lowered its $4.20 rate, from the same survey
plannedCharts.subtitle: India's 2023-24 poverty rates under the World Bank's old (2017) and new (2021) price base · same survey, same release
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Shows that a change of yardstick moved the numbers, not a change in people's lives.

plannedCharts.title: Depending on the line and the method, India's 2022-23 poverty rate is anywhere from 2% to 26%
plannedCharts.subtitle: Published estimates for 2022-23 · World Bank (direct survey) and Himanshu, Lanjouw and Schirmer (2025, bridging old and new surveys)
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Shows how much of the argument is about the line and the method.

plannedCharts.title: Between the two newest surveys, the poorest tenth's spending grew fastest
plannedCharts.subtitle: Change in average real spending by tenth of the population, HCES 2022-23 to 2023-24 · World Bank
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Shows who gained within the two comparable surveys.

plannedCharts.title: Since 1977, household spending in the national accounts has more than quadrupled. In the surveys, it has only doubled
plannedCharts.subtitle: Real GDP per person, household spending in the national accounts, and average spending in the household surveys, 1977 = 100 · World Bank · grey links join surveys that are not comparable
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Shows the gap behind the argument that surveys miss the rich.

plannedCharts.title: Money poverty is the smallest of these numbers
plannedCharts.subtitle: Six measures, each with its own population and year · child stunting NFHS-5 (2019-21), health-spending hardship (2022), World Bank measures from HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Shows what a spending line cannot see.

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
